name: Bilal Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bilal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, happy to. I'm Bilal, 27, and I work for Northfield Care Co-op, which is a not-for-profit where the care workers are members and vote on things. I share a flat near the ring road with my friend Tomasz, who's a chef.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most of my clients have dementia, so my visits are longer, usually an hour. I help with washing, meals and medication, and a lot of it is just keeping someone calm and oriented, like reminding them what day it is without making them feel stupid. I love the moments when someone suddenly remembers a song or a name. What wears me out is the evenings when a client is frightened and I have to leave on time anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that's roughly what I expect anyway. I use one of those AI apps now and then to translate a medicine leaflet for a client, and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine by me. Care was never going to be done by a chatbot. Online I'd probably post something like, good, now let's talk about paying carers properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it means my life stays pretty steady. The co-op has more clients than staff, my hours are solid, and I've got about four months saved. My clients with dementia don't need faster software. They need the same face at the door every Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my visits, keep my four regulars, and keep saving a bit each month. I'd maybe go to the co-op's member meeting and push for a pay rise now that nothing's being spent on fancy tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit relieved, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the co-op is stable. What would make you worry even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the council cut what it pays per hour. That's happened before, two years ago, and the co-op had to freeze pay. It's the money from the council, not the technology, that I watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any routine task you'd actually like AI to take off you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The care notes. We write notes after every visit, and typing them on the phone in the car takes ten minutes I'd rather spend with clients. If AI did that properly, I'd take it.

say: I'd say care was never going to be **done by a chatbot**.
I'd post that we should now talk about **paying carers** properly.
think: I think my **hours are solid**, because the co-op has more clients than staff.
I think the bigger risk is the **council** cutting what it pays per hour.
do: Keep my **four regulars** and my usual visits.
Keep **saving** a bit each month on top of four months saved.
Push for a **pay rise** at the co-op member meeting.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit **relieved** that nothing big is changing.
S0.quote: My clients with dementia don't need faster software. They need the same face at the door every Tuesday.
fieldNote: He's secure: a co-op with **more clients than staff** and four months saved.
His only worry is **council funding**, which once froze his pay.
He'd happily hand **care notes** to AI if it freed time for clients.

steps.text: Keep the same four dementia clients with weekly visits
Keep adding to savings each month
Raise a pay rise motion at the co-op member meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like it hits the office, not me. Planning, booking, answering phones, that's the co-op's back room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the co-op should use AI for the boring stuff and keep every saved penny inside the co-op. At work I'd argue that any money saved goes into longer visits. Online I'd say this is exactly why care should be owned by the people doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own job is fine for now, because no software is washing anyone. But The co-op office will get smaller, and the people who answer the phone at the co-op are my friends. That bothers me more than I expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever note-taking and rota tools the co-op brings in, once the others have tried them. I'd put forward a motion that nobody in the office is made redundant, they get moved into care or training instead. And I'd keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me, but for the place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the co-op office would you be thinking about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sandra, who does the rota. She's been there twelve years and knows which client hates men and which one needs the same carer every time. If a program does her job, I'd want her moved somewhere, not sacked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the new tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once I've seen them work. I'm not first in the queue, but I'm not last either. If it writes my notes while I drive, I'll take it.

say: I'd say the co-op should use AI for **the boring stuff** only.
I'd argue any money saved should fund **longer visits** for clients.
think: I think my **hands-on job** is fine, because no software washes anyone.
I think the **co-op office** will shrink, and those people are my friends.
do: Learn the co-op's **new note tools** once others have tried them.
Put a **no-redundancy motion** forward for office staff.
Keep **saving** monthly at the current rate.
feel: **Uneasy**, more for the co-op than for **myself**.
S1.quote: The co-op office will get smaller, and the people who answer the phone at the co-op are my friends.
fieldNote: He sees that thinking AI hits **office colleagues**, not his own visits.
His instinct is to protect others through **co-op democracy**.
He'd adopt tools **once proven**, typical of his steady approach.

steps.text: Learn the co-op's AI note tool after colleagues trial it
Propose a co-op motion moving office staff into care, not redundancy
Keep monthly savings going at the current amount

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that's a different story. Two years for the office stuff and five for my actual hands. I'd be 32 when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that care robots should only come in if the workers decide how. At the co-op I'd say we need a plan this year, not in 2030. Online I'd push for a law that care workers are retrained on full pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my hours shrink once the robots are good enough. A robot could lift my client Mr Duda out of the bath by 2031, but it won't know he only calms down to old polka records. So maybe the human bit stays, but there'd be fewer of us doing it, and less pay to go round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look at the nurse apprenticeship at the hospital, because nurses do more of the judging and talking. I'd push my savings up to six months by skipping the trip to Copenhagen. And I'd get the co-op to set up a working group on robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, because I've got some savings and a co-op behind me, but my stomach turns a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in those three years between the AI and the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn everything about dementia care that a robot can't, the talking, the calming, and get qualified in it. Then when the robots come, I'm the person who supervises how they're used with dementia clients. That's the plan anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomasz about it that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably that we're both in trouble, because a robot can chop onions too. Then we'd laugh about it and order pizza. But I'd lie awake after.

say: I'd say care robots should come in only if **workers decide how**.
I'd push for a law to retrain care workers on **full pay**.
think: I think my **hours shrink** once robots are good enough, around 2031.
I think the **human part** stays, but fewer of us share it.
do: Apply for the hospital's **nurse apprenticeship** in the first year.
Skip the **Copenhagen trip** to get savings to six months.
Set up a co-op **working group** on robots.
feel: **Anxious**, with a **turning stomach**, but not panicking.
S2.quote: A robot could lift my client Mr Duda out of the bath by 2031, but it won't know he only calms down to old polka records.
fieldNote: He uses the **three-year gap** to plan a move into dementia specialism or nursing.
Savings and the co-op give him **some control**, keeping him off alarmed.
His concrete client story shows what he thinks robots **can't do**.

steps.text: Apply for the hospital nurse apprenticeship within a year
Skip the Copenhagen trip and build six months of savings
Start a co-op working group on how robots get used

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking side and around eight for the robots. That feels more manageable. I'd be about 35.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a warning we'd be stupid to ignore. At the co-op I'd say we've got time to train people up, so let's fund it. Online I'd share stuff about how other countries handle care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's the same story with breathing room. Five years is enough time to start a nursing degree, and not enough time to stop worrying about rent. I'd still lose some hours eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time nursing degree within two years, while keeping three days a week at the co-op. I'd join the campaign for free tuition for care workers moving into nursing. And I'd stay put in the flat so rent doesn't jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I think. Worried, but with a plan, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like you said with the fast one, you'd look at nursing. Would five years make you start sooner or later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sooner, actually. With five years, starting now means I'm qualified before the robots turn up. Leaving it means competing with everyone else who suddenly wants to be a nurse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your rent while you study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gets tight. Three days of care pay covers my half with Tomasz, just about, and the savings cover the rest. If the student grant came back, it'd be easy.

say: I'd say this is a **warning** we'd be stupid to ignore.
I'd say the co-op has time to **fund training** for its members.
think: I think it's **the same story** with more breathing room.
I think five years is enough to start **a nursing degree**, but rent still worries me.
do: Start a **part-time nursing degree** within two years.
Keep **three days** a week of co-op visits for income.
Join the campaign for **free tuition** for carers moving into nursing.
feel: **Uneasy** but steadier, because I'd **have a plan**.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to start a nursing degree, and not enough time to stop worrying about rent.
fieldNote: Extra time pushes him to **start earlier**, before others rush into nursing.
He keeps care work part-time to protect his half of **the rent**.
He links personal plans to a **policy fight** over tuition.

steps.text: Start a part-time nursing degree within two years
Keep three days a week of co-op dementia visits
Campaign for free nursing tuition for care workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years for the AI, thirteen for robots. I'd be 40 by then. That feels like another life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have no excuse not to get this right. At work I'd say let's use the decade to make the co-op the best dementia service around. Online I'd be quite upbeat, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm probably okay, as long as I actually do something. Ten years of warning is a gift, and I'd hate to be the guy who spent it scrolling. The risk is I get comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job for now, and start the nursing degree in maybe three or four years. I'd add a bit more to savings each year as pay goes up. And I'd keep pushing the co-op to plan ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. A little uneasy about my own laziness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years make you more relaxed or less driven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, less driven. Ten years sounds like forever at 27. That's why I'd want a date on the calendar for applying, so I don't drift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you picture yourself at 40?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A dementia nurse, maybe running a small team in the co-op, with robots doing the heavy lifting and people doing the talking. That's the good version, anyway.

say: I'd say there's **no excuse** not to get this right with a decade.
I'd say the co-op should become the **best dementia service** around.
think: I think I'm **probably okay** if I actually act on it.
I think the real risk is that I **get comfortable** and drift.
do: Keep doing my **co-op visits** as normal for now.
Start the **nursing degree** in three or four years.
Add more to **savings** each year as pay rises.
feel: Fairly **calm**, a little **uneasy** about my own drift.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning is a gift, and I'd hate to be the guy who spent it scrolling.
fieldNote: Ten years makes him **less driven**, which he names himself.
He wants a **fixed date** to apply so he doesn't drift.
His good future is a **dementia nurse** leading people alongside robots.

steps.text: Keep doing co-op dementia visits for the next few years
Set a date to apply for a nursing degree in year three
Raise savings each year as pay goes up

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's barely time to train before the robots come. What would help is paid training for care workers to move into nursing, and a say for the co-op in how robots are used. If the machines do the lifting one day, I want the co-op members to vote on it, not some investor in another country.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the clients' families. They're the ones who'll decide whether Mum gets a robot or a person, and I don't think they've thought about it at all.

headlineQuote: If the machines do the lifting one day, I want the co-op members to vote on it, not some investor in another country.
portrait: Bilal is a **27-year-old care worker** at a not-for-profit co-op, visiting clients with **dementia**.
He shares a flat with a chef friend and has about **four months** saved.
He's **progressive** and trusts co-op democracy to protect workers, including office colleagues.
He picks up tools **once proven** and sees a path into **dementia nursing**.
He's calm in AI Plateau, uneasy in slower pictures, and **anxious** only when robots come by 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's barely time to train before robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** into nursing, and a **co-op say** in how robots are used.
